art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's art news begins close to home, at the Musée de Grenoble, and then travels out to Paris, Japan and Britain, with a little dance at the end.

The museum is where most of your options are, and they all gather around Anne Truitt and her exhibition, "Libérer la couleur". The most immediate is this afternoon: a guided tour of the show is open to the public at half past two, so if your day allows, it is a convenient way to see it with someone talking you through the work. If you would rather come at it through words, the museum library has put together a selection of books by and about Truitt, displayed alongside the exhibition. It links her paintings and sculpture with her writing, which is a lovely way to see how one practice fed the other.

And there is a date to put in your diary. On the twelfth and thirteenth of December, the actress Anne Castillo will perform readings from Truitt's journal at the museum, directed by Mathieu Barché. For someone who loves the meeting point of art and literature, a journal read aloud by an actress, in a room tied to the exhibition, sounds rather special. It is also a good reminder that this is an artist who wrote as carefully as she made.

Also at the Musée de Grenoble, a new solo exhibition opens on the fourteenth of November, devoted to Edmund Kesting. He is presented as a painter, photographer and advertising artist, which is an intriguing combination. The listing is brief, so I can't yet tell you what the show will focus on, but it may be worth watching for more details as the date approaches.

Turning to stories where art meets history, The Guardian has three pieces worth knowing about. The first is a review of Ibrahim Mahama's exhibition at the Fondation Cartier in Paris. Mahama has rebuilt a crumbling bottle plant inside the gallery and set Asante stools within it, and the show explores Ghana after colonialism. The headline suggests the future is Ghana-shaped, and the reviewer does find a sense of hope in it. If you find yourself in Paris, it sounds like a show that makes history physical, something you can walk through rather than just read about.

The second is a photo-led feature on Giada Ripa's project in Japan, which sets archive photographs from the eighteen-sixties beside modern work, so that past and present are in conversation. Woven through it is the story of one of Ripa's relatives, who became a muse to nineteenth-century artists and intellectuals. That is the stuff of a novel, frankly, and I can imagine a narrator drawing you in with exactly that kind of family thread.

The third is a gentler guide, also from The Guardian, to five free exhibitions. It includes Pia Camil's playful show on desire, Mark Leckey's more brooding work, and the photography of Cindy Sherman. The text doesn't specify the venues, so it is more a sampler of what is out there than something to plan around, but the contrast between Camil's playfulness and Leckey's brooding is a nice pairing.

Now to Britain, where two items speak to your English literature side. From the twenty-fourth of October until the twenty-eighth of February, MK Gallery in Milton Keynes hosts a thorough survey of LS Lowry. The Guardian's week-in-art column calls him the strangest and perhaps most truthful painter of modern Britain, which is a wonderful phrase to hold up against those crowded industrial streets and matchstick figures. It is far from Grenoble, of course, but it could make a good springboard for a class on British art and the way writers and painters have seen the same landscapes.

The Guardian also carries an obituary of the painter Terry Lee, written by his child. He died aged ninety-three and taught at Sheffield College of Art for almost three decades. His early work was linked to the Kitchen Sink painters, those artists of everyday, unglamorous domestic life, but over time it became more lyrical, shaped by landscape, music and literature. There is something very touching in that arc, from the gritty to the musical, and in a career where books and painting quietly fed one another.

Finally, a nod to dance, which I know you enjoy. The Guardian looks at Life magazine's photo spreads on dance, from George Balanchine to the Rockettes, and reads them as a mirror of a changing America. The piece blends the history of photojournalism with the story of dance, though it does also touch on social politics, so you may want to dip in with that in mind. The images alone, from proms to parties, sound like a rich way to see how people moved, and what that said about them.

So there is plenty for you today: Truitt close by this afternoon and again in December, Kesting to come in November, and a few stories further afield. I hope the light over Belledonne is kind to you as you choose.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's briefing begins close to home, at the Musée de Grenoble, where one artist's colour and words take centre stage, and then travels out to Paris, Japan, Milton Keynes and the dancefloors of America.

Let me start with the thing you could do this very afternoon. At half past two today, the Musée de Grenoble is offering a guided tour of its Anne Truitt exhibition, which is called "Libérer la couleur", or freeing colour. The tour is open to the public, so if your Friday timetable allows, it is a convenient way to see the show with someone talking you through it. A guided visit is often the best way into an artist whose work you do not already know well, because a good guide gives you a way of looking before you start wandering the rooms alone.

What makes this exhibition especially interesting for you is that Truitt is an artist who wrote as well as made. The museum's library has put together a selection of books by and about her, shown alongside the exhibition. The selection connects her paintings and sculpture with her writing, so you can come out of the galleries and sit down with the words behind the work. That feels like an invitation to do exactly what you like doing best: look at a picture, then read your way around it.

And the writing does not stop there. On the twelfth and thirteenth of December, the museum is staging readings from Anne Truitt's journal. The actress Anne Castillo will perform them, directed by Mathieu Barché, and the sessions are tied to the exhibition. A journal read aloud by an actress, in a room where the artist's work is on the walls, sounds like a lovely way to hear a voice that has so far come to us only through the page and the object. If you are thinking of bringing a class, or a colleague from the department, it is worth marking those dates now, since it is a good few weeks away and weekends in December tend to fill quickly. I would also say it makes an interesting companion for the idea of the artist as narrator, which you could easily imagine placing beside your work on first-person voices with older pupils.

Also at the Musée de Grenoble, and a little further off, is a solo exhibition on Edmund Kesting, opening on the fourteenth of November. He is presented as a painter, a photographer and an advertising artist, which is an intriguing combination, the fine and the commercial living in one career. The listing is very brief, though, so I cannot yet tell you what the show will focus on. I would keep an eye on the museum's announcements nearer the time. For now, it is simply a date and a promising trio of descriptions.

So, for Grenoble, the picture is this: Truitt today and through the season, with her journal brought to life in December, and Kesting arriving in mid November.

Now let me move across the Channel, because there are a couple of items that sit well with your British section. The first is the Lowry exhibition, which opens tomorrow, the twenty-fourth of October, and runs until the twenty-eighth of February at MK Gallery in Milton Keynes. The Guardian's week-in-art column describes it as a thorough survey of LS Lowry, whom it calls the strangest and perhaps most truthful painter of modern Britain. I rather like that phrase, the strangest and the most truthful, because it holds together two things we do not always expect to find together. Lowry's crowded streets and factory chimneys, those figures that seem both ordinary and slightly unreal, have always had something of the storyteller about them. Milton Keynes is of course a long way from the Grésivaudan, but if you are in England over the Christmas holidays, or if any of your pupils are, the show runs well into the new year, so there is time. And even from a distance, it is a good name to bring into a lesson on how writers and painters have portrayed industrial Britain.

The same column mentions, in its headline, that pop goes kinky and the wild man of Florence is tamed, which tells us only that the week is full of other shows, though the text we have gives no more detail on those.

Staying in Britain, there is a gentler piece in The Guardian, an obituary of the painter Terry Lee, written by his child. He died at the age of ninety-three, and he taught at Sheffield College of Art for almost three decades, so there will be a great many former students who remember him. His early work was linked to the Kitchen Sink painters, the group known for their gritty, domestic realism. But over time his painting became more lyrical, and the obituary says it was shaped by landscape, by music and by literature. I find that a touching trajectory, from the hard edge of everyday life towards something more musical. It is a small portrait of how a painter can be quietly formed by the poems and the pieces of music he loves. It is the sort of life story that might make a good short reading for older pupils interested in the relationship between the arts, and it comes with the added warmth of being written by someone who knew him as a parent.

Let me turn now to Paris, where The Guardian reviews an exhibition by Ibrahim Mahama at the Fondation Cartier. The headline asks why a crumbling bottle plant has been rebuilt in Paris, and the answer is that the show brings a whole factory into the gallery. Alongside it are Asante stools, and together they explore Ghana after colonialism. The reviewer calls the show stunning and suggests that the future may be Ghana-shaped. What struck me in the review is that it finds a sense of hope in the exhibition. That is not a given with work about colonial history, which can easily be elegiac or angry, and it is encouraging to read about a show that looks forward as well as back. Since you enjoy novels that teach history better than history essays, this is the kind of exhibition that does something similar in three dimensions: it lets you stand inside a piece of the past and feel what it carries. If you are ever in Paris with a free day, the Fondation Cartier is the address to remember. I would add that the review is the only source I have for the show, so I cannot tell you about opening hours or dates, which are worth checking before you plan a trip.

The Guardian also has a photo-led feature that I think you will enjoy, on a project by Giada Ripa. She sets archive photographs of Japan from the eighteen-sixties beside modern work, so that you can walk, in the words of the piece, between Japan's past and present. There is also a story woven through it, that of a relative of hers who became a muse to nineteenth-century artists and intellectuals. A muse is, of course, one of those figures who sits at the edge of the history books and in the middle of the novels, and this feels like a story with real narrative pull. Pictures from a century and a half ago placed beside today's images, and a family tale behind them: it has the structure of a good novel, where a present-day narrator goes looking for an ancestor. It is a piece to look at slowly, with a cup of tea.

If you like the idea of seeing exhibitions without spending anything, there is a guide in The Guardian to five free shows. It mentions Pia Camil's playful show on desire, Mark Leckey's more brooding work, and Cindy Sherman's photography, with a nod in the headline to Sherman's plump pearls and a hypnotic apocalypse. I should be honest that the text I have does not say where these exhibitions are, so I cannot tell you which city or gallery each one belongs to. As a snapshot of what is going on in contemporary art, though, it gives a nice contrast: Camil playful, Leckey brooding, Sherman with her unmistakable eye for costume and character. Sherman in particular might interest you, since her photographs are so much about invented people, each picture a kind of character study without words, and you could imagine setting them beside a passage of fiction to see what narrators and faces have in common.

And finally, something for the dance lover in you. The Guardian looks at Life magazine's photo spreads on dance, ranging from George Balanchine to the Rockettes, and reads them as a mirror of changing American life. There are proms and parties, and the piece also touches on gender politics, so it does lean a little towards the social side. But it is above all a story about photojournalism and dance, and about how a magazine used pictures of bodies in motion to tell a country about itself. Balanchine and the Rockettes are an interesting pairing, the austere and the glittering sharing the same pages. If you enjoy documentaries about dance, you may find that these pictures have a similar pleasure: they catch a moment of movement and let you imagine the music.

So, to bring the threads together. Close to home, you have Anne Truitt's colour and words at the Musée de Grenoble, with a tour today, a library selection to browse, and the journal readings in December, followed by Kesting in November. Further afield, Lowry begins tomorrow in Milton Keynes, a painter's lifetime is remembered in Terry Lee's obituary, Ibrahim Mahama brings a Ghanaian factory to Paris, Giada Ripa pairs old and new Japan, there are five free exhibitions to hunt down, and Life magazine's dancers whirl across the page.

Enjoy the afternoon with Anne Truitt, Yamuna, and may there be a good colour waiting for you around every corner.

literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's literary news has a pleasing shape: a novel that has become an opera, three very different narrators, some stories of place and music, and a couple of readers talking about the books that made them.

Let me start with the thread that runs through several pieces: George Saunders's "Lincoln in the Bardo", which won the Booker Prize in twenty seventeen. Missy Mazzoli's opera of the same name has now premiered at the Metropolitan Opera. The story that inspired it is the one you will know: Abraham Lincoln's sorrow at a family tomb, and the strange, crowded, experimental novel Saunders built around it. The report I found on the premiere is rather thin and gives no date, but the Washington Post has a more satisfying piece. It looks closely at how Saunders found the language for what it calls a president's operatic grief. The interest there is in how a novel's style, with all its voices, could become music almost naturally. If you ever teach extracts from the book, that piece might be a good companion, because it is really about how words carry feeling.

That brings me to voice, which is the heart of three other items this morning. The Guardian reviews "Female Life on Planet Earth" by Laleh Khadivi. Its narrator, Heti, is an Iranian-American mother living in Los Angeles who begins to suspect that her late mother may have been an enforcer of the Iranian revolution. So it is a novel about inheritance and identity, and about what you do with a family history that turns out to be darker and more complicated than you were told. The reviewer presents Heti as a strong and complicated presence, which is always the thing that draws you in.

Then there is Emma Cline, who has made her name writing troubled young women. In her new novel, "Switzy", she does something quite different and writes from inside a man with dementia. The Conversation looks at the book, and what stands out is the choice of point of view. A narrator whose grip on the world is loosening is a hard thing to do well on the page, and it is interesting to see a writer step so far outside her usual territory.

And for something much lighter, the Guardian reviews the audiobook of "Black Bag" by Luke Kennard, which was shortlisted for the Booker Prize. It is a campus comedy about an unnamed, out-of-work actor who is hired to live inside a black leather bag. Kennard reads it himself, and the reviewer is full of praise for his voice and his comic timing. It is a reminder that a narrator can be a literal voice as well as a literary one, and that a comic novel can come alive in the ear.

Now to a few pieces about literary history, place and music. The New Yorker has a story with a wonderful hook, called "Hemingway's Vendetta". In nineteen fifty-two, Hemingway read a novel by a thirty-year-old Yale graduate who was also a former bullfighter. He decided the young man was a fraud, and then waged a secret campaign against him. I only have the standfirst, so I can't tell you how it unfolds, but the setup alone is irresistible, a great writer, a younger rival and a lot of wounded pride.

From Literary Hub comes a lovely piece of reminiscence, "What It Was Like to See Nina Simone at the Village Gate", from around nineteen sixty-one. The writer recalls the hum of the audience and the announcement made just before she came on stage. It is a short piece, but it has that sense of a room and a moment that you can almost step into, with the music still to come.

Literary Hub also has a debut novelist writing about how Salem Harbor and Hawthorne's "The House of the Seven Gables" shaped her first book. She links a real house, colonial history and fiction, and it is a good example of how a place can pull a story out of a writer. Hawthorne's old house becomes a doorway into the past, and I think you would enjoy the way she describes it.

To finish, two items about readers and writers at the lighter end. The Guardian has an interview with Bonnie Garmus, author of "Lessons in Chemistry", in which she talks about the books that shaped her. They run from "Fun with Dick and Jane" to "Harriet the Spy" and the novels of Louisa May Alcott. She also says she wrote her first novel at twelve, and that it has not yet found a publisher, which made me smile. It is a warm, reader-to-reader conversation, the sort that makes you want to go back to your own childhood shelves.

And Helen Fielding has launched a new prize for northern comedy writing, named for Bridget Jones. It asks for one thousand words of first-person prose from northern England. It is modelled on the anonymous diary columns that first introduced Bridget to the world, and it is aimed at unknown voices. Given that so much of today's news is about the pull of a strong narrator, it feels fitting that a prize should be built around exactly that: a distinctive voice, a small canvas and a lot of nerve. Your students might even like the idea of trying it, though I should say I have no further details beyond what I have told you.

If you spot one thread across all of this, it is that stories travel, from page to stage, from childhood shelves to grown-up careers, from a smoky club to a few paragraphs of memory.

Enjoy your morning, and I hope there is a good book waiting for you by the window.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's literary news is full of voices: narrators who speak from inside grief, memory, a leather bag, and a house by the sea, and a few readers talking about the books that made them.

Let me begin with the story that has two outlets talking, and which seems made for you. George Saunders's novel "Lincoln in the Bardo", which won the Booker Prize in twenty seventeen, has now become an opera. Missy Mazzoli's setting of it has premiered at the Metropolitan Opera. The report I have seen, a post on Facebook, is brief and gives no premiere date, so I won't pretend to details I don't have. What it does confirm is the starting point: the story of Abraham Lincoln's sorrow at a family tomb, which inspired Saunders's experimental novel, and which now reaches the stage in song.

The more substantial piece comes from The Washington Post, which looks closely at how Saunders found the language for what it calls a president's operatic grief. I find that framing rather lovely, because the grief was always operatic in a sense. The novel was already a kind of chorus, an experiment in many voices speaking at once around one sorrowing man. So the idea that it was waiting to become music has a certain logic. The Post is interested in the writing itself: how a novel's style could carry so much feeling that composing it into an opera feels less like an adaptation and more like a continuation. If you ever teach the book, or a passage from it, this is the sort of article that might send you back to the page to listen for the rhythm, asking which lines already sound like arias, and which sound like a crowd murmuring in the dark.

From a famous experiment in voice, let me move to three new books that all hinge on who is telling the story and how.

The Guardian reviews "Female Life on Planet Earth" by Laleh Khadivi. Its narrator, Heti, is an Iranian-American mother living in Los Angeles. She learns that her late mother may have been an enforcer of the Iranian revolution. It's a premise that turns a family inheritance into a question: what do you do with a parent you thought you knew, once the past has been opened up? The review presents it as a novel about inheritance and identity, with a strong and complicated narrator. For a reader like you, who likes to step into a story without needing to know the culture first, that sounds promising. A personal discovery gives you a way into a historical upheaval, because you learn about the revolution as Heti does, through the unsettling question of what her mother did. That is the kind of fiction that can teach history in a way essays rarely manage.

Then there's Emma Cline, who is known, as The Conversation puts it, for her troubled young women. In her new novel "Switzy", she does something different. She writes from inside a man with dementia. The Conversation's piece, whether you read it as a review or an essay, treats the change of narrator as the heart of the book. I think that's right. Dementia is a hard thing to render from the inside, because the narrator's grip on time, on names and on reality is exactly what's loosening, and so the prose itself has to do the work. A writer who has built her reputation on one kind of character, deliberately stepping into another kind of consciousness, is always interesting. It would make a good pairing for pupils with any text where a narrator's reliability is in question, if you wanted to talk about what we trust a voice to tell us.

The third voice is a comic one, and it arrives by audiobook. The Guardian reviews Luke Kennard's "Black Bag", which was shortlisted for the Booker Prize, and which Kennard narrates himself. The novel is a campus comedy about an unnamed, out-of-work actor who is hired to live inside a black leather bag. I'll admit that sentence made me smile on its own. The Guardian calls it brilliant, and the praise is particularly for the narration: the voice and the comic timing. It's a useful reminder that comedy on the page is often a matter of rhythm, the pause before the punchline, and that an author reading his own work can sometimes find a beat that a silent reader would miss. If you have a long drive down into the Grésivaudan, this might be good company.

Let me turn now to books that are about other books, and about place and history.

The New Yorker has a piece called "Hemingway's Vendetta", and although I only have the standfirst to go on, the hook is a good one. In nineteen fifty-two, Hemingway read a novel by a thirty-year-old Yale graduate who was also a former bullfighter. He dismissed the young man as a fraud, and then, the piece says, waged a secret campaign against him. I can't tell you more than that, because the text I have stops there, and I'd rather not guess at how the story ends. But it has the shape of a good literary tale: a towering figure, a younger rival, a private grudge pursued in secret. It also raises a question that every teacher of literature will recognise, which is how much a writer's reputation and temperament shape how we read their judgments of others. It may be worth looking up in full.

On a gentler note, Literary Hub has a debut novelist describing how a love of Salem, and of Hawthorne's "The House of Seven Gables", shaped her first book. She writes about Salem Harbor and about a real house, and how colonial history and fiction can grow out of the same place. I like this sort of essay because it shows the way a novel is often born from a particular spot on the map, and from a particular book that the writer read at the right moment. Hawthorne's house, as she tells it, becomes a kind of doorway, and her own novel steps through. If you are ever thinking about how to get pupils to write fiction rooted in a place they know, whether a harbour, an old house or a mountain village, this is a nice model of how an inspiration can be both a landscape and a text.

Also from Literary Hub, and perhaps the most musical piece of the day, is a reminiscence of seeing Nina Simone at the Village Gate around nineteen sixty-one. The writer remembers the hum of the audience, that low murmur of a room waiting, and the announcement made before she took the stage. I don't have more of the text than that, so I can't tell you what was said. But even from those details you can feel the piece's method: it begins not with the performer but with the room, with the sounds of anticipation, and lets the reader stand among the crowd before anything happens. It is a lovely example of how prose can recreate a concert, and a sense of a place and a moment in history. For someone who loves both classical music documentaries and the written word, it sits at the crossing point nicely.

Finally, a few pieces that are about readers and writers more than about any single book.

The Guardian talks to Bonnie Garmus, the author of "Lessons in Chemistry". The interview, in the paper's series on authors and their reading, takes her back to her earliest reading memories. She mentions "Fun with Dick and Jane", then "Harriet the Spy", and Louisa May Alcott. The headline carries a nice detail: she says she wrote her first novel at twelve, and that it has not yet found a publisher. It's a warm, reader-to-reader conversation, and I think it captures something true: that the books we meet as children are so often the ones that teach us what a story is. Harriet the Spy, in particular, is a narrator who watches and writes things down, and that seems a fitting early companion for someone who went on to write novels. It's the sort of interview that might make a pleasant opening to a lesson on pupils' own first reading memories, if you wanted to try that.

And last, something light and rather playful. Helen Fielding has launched a prize for northern comedy writing, named for her most famous creation, Bridget Jones. It asks for a thousand words of first-person prose from northern England. The model, as The Guardian explains, is the anonymous diary columns that first introduced Bridget Jones to readers. I like the idea very much. It puts the emphasis on an unmistakable voice rather than a polished plot, and it is aimed at unknown writers, people who haven't yet been published. A thousand words is a good size for a classroom exercise too: long enough to build a narrator, short enough to finish. If any of your première pupils enjoy writing in a distinctive first-person voice, it might at least be a model to borrow, even if the prize itself is for northern writers.

If I step back, there is a pleasing thread running through today. Saunders gave a president's grief many voices, and now Mazzoli gives it song. Khadivi, Cline and Kennard each ask us to inhabit a narrator who is unsettled, whether by a secret in the family, by a failing memory, or by a rather absurd job. Hawthorne's house and Nina Simone's audience both remind us how much a place can hold. And from Bonnie Garmus to Helen Fielding, there is the simple pleasure of the voices that start us reading, and writing, in the first place.

That's the literature briefing for today, Yamuna. I hope there's a good book, and perhaps a good cup of tea, waiting for you this evening.

around.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Friday the twenty-third of October, and this is a gentle round-up of what's happening around you, with a good deal of woodland, a little poetry and some history thrown in.

Let me begin with today, and with something close to home. This afternoon, from two o'clock until half past four, at the Barioz nordic area in Crêts en Belledonne, you can try a marteloscope, which is a hands-on way of stepping into a forester's shoes. The meeting point is the car park by the Foyer de Fond du Barioz. It belongs to the Forestivités, the autumn festival devoted to the forest, and it's the closest event to Les Adrets that I have for you today. If the afternoon is fine, it sounds like a pleasant way to be out among the trees in their autumn colours, and perhaps to see the woods with a more practical eye than usual.

The Forestivités themselves stretch well beyond this one afternoon. The festival began on the eighteenth of October and runs until the first of November, and it is spread across several places. In Allevard, there is a free programme under way for the whole fortnight. In Grenoble, too, the Forestivités offer a set of free events over the same dates. I have to be honest that the listings for both are rather thin and don't spell out exactly what is on each day, so it would be worth a glance at the local agenda before you set off, particularly if you're hoping for something specific. But the fact that it's free and spans two weeks, with the half-term holidays so near, makes it easy to fit in on a day when the weather is kind.

Now for something to do with words. On the third of November, at eight in the evening, the Hexagone, the scène nationale in Meylan, presents Limbus, by the company éOle. It's described as a theatrical and cinematic concert, in the manner of a road trip, and it draws on two texts by Henri Michaux: L'infini turbulent and Connaissance par les gouffres. I thought of you at once, because Michaux is such a singular writer, and these are two of his explorations of inner worlds, of the strange and the boundless. To hear his language carried by music and image, rather than read quietly on the page, sounds like an evening that could be both unsettling and beautiful. It's a little over a week away, so it's worth thinking about booking soon, though I don't have any details on tickets.

Staying in Grenoble, there is a cultural event running from yesterday until Sunday the twenty-fifth, called Aime moi... Si tu peux! The listing gives no word about whether it is theatre, music or something else entirely, so I can only point you towards the title, which has a certain playful challenge to it. If your curiosity is piqued, it's a short window, with just today, tomorrow and Sunday left.

Also in Grenoble, and quieter, is Le mois des p'tits lecteurs, a free reading month for children that runs through all of October. It has only a week left, and the listing doesn't say much about what it offers. Still, as a teacher, you might find it interesting to see how the city encourages young readers, even if your own students are a good deal older than the audience it has in mind.

On a warmer, more human note, Le Dauphiné Libéré has a story about the Bedouin association C'est Normal, which is introducing its Savoyard neighbours to dance. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you more about the form the dance takes or where it's happening. But the idea is lovely: a community sharing movement, and a cultural exchange that begins with the body rather than with words. Given your fondness for dance and for good news, I thought it deserved a mention, and it might be worth looking up the full article.

For history, there is an exhibition at Saint-Martin-d'Hères, on the Grenoble side of the valley, called À la conquête de l'eau aux dix-neuvième et vingtième siècles en Isère. It opened on the nineteenth of September and runs until the third of April next year, so there is plenty of time, and entry is free. It looks at how water was tamed and used in Isère over those two centuries. In a region of mountains, torrents and rivers, that is a story with real drama in it, and I can imagine it pairing nicely with the novels and documents of the period. The listing doesn't give details of what's on show, but the long run means you can choose a quiet weekend rather than rush.

Finally, two festivals for younger audiences, both in full swing. In Saint-Martin-d'Hères, the twenty-fifth Fête du Cinéma d'animation runs from the eleventh of October until the first of November. The programme isn't detailed in the listing, but a twenty-fifth edition suggests a festival with some history behind it. And in Villard-Bonnot, in the Grésivaudan, the twenty-eighth Festival du Film pour Enfants runs from the nineteenth to the twenty-eighth of October. Again there is no programme given, but if you have younger relatives, or friends with children, around the holidays, both could be worth passing on. And since the animation festival has a week longer to run, it gives you more room to plan.

So, in short: the forest today at Barioz, the Forestivités in Allevard and Grenoble until the first of November, Michaux at the Hexagone on the third, and a long, quiet exhibition on water whenever the mood takes you.

I hope the day treats you kindly, and that there's a little woodland air in it somewhere.

Let me start with the one thing happening today, and it's very close to home. This afternoon, the twenty-third of October, from two o'clock until half past four, there is a marteloscope at the Barioz nordic area in Crêts en Belledonne. The meeting point is the car park of the Foyer de Fond du Barioz. A marteloscope, in case the word is new, lets visitors step into the shoes of a forester, and this one is a hands-on, outdoors session. It belongs to the Forestivités festival, and it's the nearest event on the list to Les Adrets. If the afternoon is free and the weather is kind, it sounds like a pleasant way to spend a couple of hours among the trees of Belledonne.

The Forestivités themselves are a wider affair. The autumn festival began on the eighteenth of October and runs until the first of November, with free events listed both in Allevard and in Grenoble. I should be honest that the listings for these two are thin. They give the dates and the fact that entry is free, but no programme. So it's worth looking at the local agenda for Allevard or Grenoble to see what is actually on each day. Still, with the festival running for two weeks, there is a good chance of finding something that fits a weekend or an afternoon off.

Now for something a little more literary, and I suspect it will appeal to you. On the third of November, at eight in the evening, the Hexagone, the Scène nationale in Meylan, presents Limbus, by éOle. It's described as a theatrical and cinematic concert, in the spirit of a road trip. The text it draws on is Henri Michaux: L'infini turbulent and Connaissance par les gouffres. So this is music, image and theatre all gathered around some of the most unusual poetic language in French. For someone who loves prose that works as music, it looks like a promising evening, and it's close enough to Grenoble to be an easy trip down the valley. It's still eleven days away, so there's time to think about booking.

On the subject of dance, there's a warm story in Le Dauphiné Libéré. The Bedouin association C'est Normal is introducing its Savoyard neighbours to dance. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you more about how it works or where the sessions take place. But the idea of a community sharing its movement and traditions with the people next door is a nice one, and it's the sort of good news that's pleasant to start the day with.

For something with more historical depth, there is a free exhibition in Saint-Martin-d'Hères called A la conquête de l'eau aux dix-neuvième et vingtième siècles en Isère. It has been open since the nineteenth of September and runs all the way to the third of April, 2027, so there is no rush at all. It traces how people in Isère tamed and used water over those two centuries. In a département shaped by mountains, rivers and torrents, that's a story with plenty of human interest, and I can imagine it pairing well with novels and documents from the period. Being free and open for more than six months, it's a good one to keep in your back pocket for a quiet weekend.

Saint-Martin-d'Hères has another event on at the moment: the twenty-fifth Fête du Cinéma d'animation, which began on the eleventh of October and continues until the first of November. It's an animation festival, and the listing doesn't give a programme, so I can't tell you what's showing. But a twenty-fifth edition is a real milestone, and it's open for another ten days or so.

Children's culture is well represented too, which might be useful for a teacher. In Villard-Bonnot, the twenty-eighth Festival du Film pour Enfants runs from the nineteenth to the twenty-eighth of October. Again, I have no details of the films, only the dates and the place, so it would be wise to check the programme before planning a visit. Meanwhile, in Grenoble, Le mois des p'tits lecteurs, a free reading month for young readers, takes place throughout October. There's very little information about what it involves, but with only a week of the month left, any visit would need to be soon. If you're looking for ideas about bringing young people and books together, it may be worth a look.

One more entry to mention is in Grenoble: a cultural event called Aime moi... Si tu peux ! It runs from the twenty-second to the twenty-fifth of October, so today, tomorrow and Sunday are still to come. The listing says nothing about whether it's theatre, music or something else, so I can't describe it. The title is intriguing enough to make me curious, though, and a quick search might reveal more.

To pull the week together: if you want to be outdoors, this afternoon's marteloscope at Barioz is the clear choice, and the Forestivités continue in Allevard and Grenoble until the first of November. For something quieter, the water exhibition in Saint-Martin-d'Hères has months to run. And for an evening of language and music, mark the third of November for Limbus in Meylan.

That's the picture for this morning, and I hope some of it tempts you out into the autumn air.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. The last two days have brought a good deal of Shakespeare, a little Atwood and Butler, and some Austen, so let me take it by theme.

I'll start with the oral list, where two of your authors turned up. Resilience has published an excerpt from a book called Science Fiction Ecologies, which looks at how Octavia Butler used science fiction to think through ecological collapse. It connects directly to Parable of the Sower, and it could be useful if you want to introduce your students to ecocriticism. It would give them a way of reading the novel's landscapes and its sense of a world coming apart as more than just a dystopian backdrop. It's an excerpt, so you can sample the argument without committing to the whole book.

Margaret Atwood appears too, in a review from Great British Life. The production is at York Theatre Royal, and it brings together her Penelopiad and a piece called Her Story, alongside The Odyssey. I should say the text we have is only the title, so I can't tell you much about the staging. Still, the idea is appealing: myth retold from a woman's point of view, with Penelope given a voice that Homer never gave her. For students who know The Handmaid's Tale, it's a nice way to show Atwood returning again and again to the question of who gets to tell the story.

Staying with retellings, The Guardian has an interview with the novelist Diana Reid, who has been adapting Sense and Sensibility. Her title quote is "Jane Austen is for everyone," and the piece also notes that her accent surprised British audiences. It isn't a set text for you, but Emma is on your oral list, and the interview is a pleasant prompt for thinking about how Austen travels, across countries, accents and centuries, and what an adapter keeps or changes along the way.

Now to Hamlet, which dominates the news this week, and rightly so, since it's on the session 2027 programme. Several pieces might help, from the practical to the playful.

Let me begin with the one I think is most useful for teaching. The A.V. Club has an interview with the author Kat Dunn, whose book Rottenheart takes a queer approach to Hamlet. She also talks about her favourite Gothic novels. It's a good read on how a contemporary writer takes a very familiar play and bends it, which may suit your seconde and première classes as a way into asking what a reading of Hamlet actually is. The Gothic thread is a bonus, since Hamlet's ghost, its poisoned court and its madness have always sat comfortably in that tradition.

Next, a cluster from New Jersey. NewJerseyStage.com describes Shakespeare Theatre NJ's Hamlet as a treat for the Halloween season, which is a neat reminder of how naturally the play fits a spooky mood. BroadwayWorld has also shared the trailer for the same company's production, as a video. I don't have dates or other details, but a trailer is short and could work as a classroom starter. You might show it and ask your students what the production emphasises, whether that's the ghost, the madness or the court, and whether that matches their own reading.

There's also a gentler story from the United States. TheUnion.com reports that the longtime local director John Deaderick is taking his final curtain call with a production of Hamlet. The text gives no date or venue, so it's more of a human-interest note than something to plan around. But there's something fitting about a director choosing this play for a farewell, and it might make a small aside for students about why Hamlet is the role, and the play, that people return to at the end of a career.

Then there's NT News, which carries a piece on a modern stage Hamlet under the headline "To scroll or not to scroll." The text is brief, but the wordplay on "to be or not to be" suggests a production with a contemporary, screen-minded angle. It could make a lively discussion starter: what does it do to the soliloquies if we update the world around them? I'd treat it as a prompt rather than a source, given how little detail we have.

Moving from tragedy to comedy, Theatre and Tonic has reviewed Twelfth Night at the Crucible Theatre in Sheffield. This is also on the 2027 programme, and a review is a helpful way to see how the text plays in performance: how the comedy and the melancholy are balanced, and how a director handles Viola's disguise and Malvolio's humiliation. If you're building a lesson on staging and interpretation, a review like this gives you a working critic's vocabulary to borrow, and lets students compare it with their own reading of the scenes.

Finally, something for the dance lover in you. Place des Arts has a piece on Guillaume Côté's Midsummer Night Dreams, headlined "Love, set free," which brings Shakespeare's comedy into ballet. The text we have is only the headline, so I can't say more about the choreography. But it's an appealing idea, and a lovely way to ask students how a story told without words can still carry Shakespeare's tangle of love and confusion. It isn't on your programme, but the question of what survives when the language is removed is a good one for any class studying the plays.

If I had to pick one thing to look at over a cup of tea, it would be the Kat Dunn interview, with the Butler excerpt a close second. Enjoy the day, and may your Hamlets all be well-spoken.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quiet couple of days for official BFI news, but there's a good bundle of material around the works on your lists, with a strong Hamlet thread, a Twelfth Night review, and a few pieces on your oral-theme authors that could be useful as the term settles in.

I'll start with the oral themes, because three items touch authors on that list. The first is a book excerpt published by Resilience, from a volume called Science Fiction Ecologies. It looks at how Octavia Butler used science fiction to think through ecological collapse. That connects directly to Parable of the Sower, which sits on your oral list. I haven't been given the full text, only the description, so I can't tell you which passages or arguments the excerpt picks out. But the framing is the useful part. Butler is so often taught as a dystopian writer, or as a writer about society breaking down, and this piece invites students to read the novel as an ecological text too. If you're looking for a way into ecocriticism with première students, it could be a short, serious companion to the novel. You might ask them to track how the landscape appears in Lauren's journal entries: the heat, the walls, the scarcity. Then ask whether the environment in the novel is background or a character in its own right. That is a question students can answer from the text, and the excerpt gives you a critical vocabulary to support it, without anyone needing to know the theory first.

Staying with the oral list, Great British Life has a review of a production at York Theatre Royal that brings together Margaret Atwood's The Penelopiad and a piece called Her Story, alongside The Odyssey. I should be honest that all I have is the headline, so I can't tell you how the staging works, who directs, or how the three pieces fit together. But the idea itself is worth a moment. The Penelopiad is Atwood retelling the Odysseus story from Penelope's side, and from the voices of her hanged maids. Atwood is on your oral-theme list through The Handmaid's Tale, so this is a way of showing students that her interest in women's voices, and in who is allowed to tell the story, runs well beyond Gilead. It would make a neat bridge. You could ask what changes when a narrator who was silenced in the original is given the floor. That question applies to Offred as much as to Penelope. And if a class has read any Homer in translation, even a short extract, the comparison becomes concrete very quickly. It's also a reminder that these texts keep being restaged, which is a lovely thing to tell students who think of set books as museum pieces.

The third item in this group is a Guardian interview with the novelist Diana Reid, who has been adapting Sense and Sensibility. The headline carries her line that Jane Austen is for everyone, and the piece also notes that her accent surprised British audiences. Austen herself isn't on the oral list through this novel; Emma is. But the interview is about how an adaptation travels, who is doing the adapting, and who gets to claim a classic, and that applies neatly to Emma. A class might compare how a story of manners and money can be moved into another voice or another place while staying recognisably itself. I don't have the details of the adaptation beyond the headline, so I'd treat this as a pleasant read for you, with a possible discussion prompt attached. I'd also say it echoes a question you may already put to students: what do we mean by faithful, when we say an adaptation is faithful?

Now to the largest group, which is Hamlet. It's on the session twenty twenty-seven programme, and this week there are no fewer than five pieces about productions or interpretations. They vary a lot in how much they tell us, so let me take them in order of usefulness.

The most substantial is the A.V. Club interview with the author Kat Dunn, in which she talks about queering Hamlet and about her favourite Gothic novels. The headline mentions Rottenheart, which is the work she is being interviewed about. I don't have more than the description, so I can't quote her. But the angle is rich for your seconde and première classes. Hamlet has long invited readings that push at the edges of what the play seems to say: about Hamlet's relationships with Ophelia, Horatio and Gertrude, about secrecy and performance, about who is allowed to speak openly in Elsinore. An author reimagining the play from a queer perspective is a good example of the creative critical reading that your students are asked to produce in their own way. It also lets you point out that interpretation can be an act of writing as well as an essay. And the Gothic strand is a good hook. A ghost, a decaying court, a mind coming apart: Hamlet has a lot in common with the Gothic tradition, and your students will recognise that atmosphere. If you teach Great Expectations alongside it, the same vocabulary of ghosts, decay and haunted houses will apply to Miss Havisham's Satis House. That kind of link across two set books is exactly what students find hard to make unprompted, so having an author naming Gothic influences in an easy conversational interview is a gift.

Then there are three items about Shakespeare Theatre New Jersey's Hamlet, though only two are about the same production, so let me separate them. NewJerseyStage reports on Shakespeare Theatre NJ's Hamlet, presenting it as a treat for the Halloween season. BroadwayWorld, meanwhile, shares a video trailer for a Hamlet by the Shakespeare Theatre of New Jersey. These look to be the same company and the same production, one a piece of coverage and the other a trailer, though I can't confirm the dates from what I have. The Halloween framing is interesting in itself, and it's timely, since half term is nearly upon us. It's a reminder of how naturally Hamlet fits a season of ghosts and dark nights. It begins with a ghost on the battlements, after all. You might ask students why the play opens in cold and darkness, with nervous soldiers rather than the prince, and what Shakespeare gains by starting with fear before character. As for the trailer, I'd say it's worth watching first before deciding. A trailer is a very short, compressed piece of interpretation. It chooses which lines, images and moods to sell. That makes it a good quick exercise: if you had ninety seconds to represent your reading of Hamlet, what would you show? I haven't seen it, so I can't promise it's classroom-ready, but as a model of a stage interpretation of a set text it has potential.

Next is a piece from NT News headed with the question: to scroll or not to scroll, with the subtitle that a modern Hamlet hits the stage. The text I have is brief, so I can't tell you how phones or screens figure in the production. But the headline's joke is a good one, turning the most famous line in English drama into a comment on our habits with our phones. For students, that's a very accessible way into the soliloquy. You can ask what the original question is really about, and why it still sounds modern. The wordplay also shows how one speech can be borrowed, parodied and reused, and that is a useful lesson about how deeply Hamlet has seeped into everyday language. It might make a lively five-minute starter: let students suggest their own contemporary versions of the dilemma, and then bring them back to the actual lines to see what the original is doing that the joke leaves out.

The last Hamlet item is a local report from TheUnion.com, saying that the longtime director John Deaderick will take his final curtain call with a production of Hamlet. There's no date or venue in the text I have, so I can't tell you more. It's a gentle story, and probably not one to bring into class as such, but there's something nice in it. A director choosing Hamlet to end a career says something about the play's place in theatre life: it's the piece people return to, perhaps as a kind of summing up. If you ever want to talk with older students about why some texts become the ones people come back to at turning points, it offers a small, human example.

That brings us to the other Shakespeare items, which are about comedy rather than tragedy. Theatre and Tonic has a review of Twelfth Night at the Crucible Theatre in Sheffield. Twelfth Night is on your session twenty twenty-seven list, so this is directly relevant. I only have the description, which says it gives a sense of how the text works on stage, so I can't tell you about casting, design or setting choices. But reviews like this are a good teaching resource in their own right. They show students how a play is talked about by people who watch it as an event, not just read it. You could give a class a short extract from a review and ask what the reviewer is praising or criticising, and then compare that with their own reading of the scene. With Twelfth Night, the questions that matter most are about tone: how much of the play is joyous, how much is cruel, and how a director balances Malvolio's humiliation against the festive atmosphere. A review of any production will have taken a view on this, even if only implicitly, and that gives students something to push against.

Finally, a piece for you as much as for your classes. Place des Arts has a feature on Guillaume Côté's dance work Midsummer Night Dreams, under the headline Love, set free. It brings Shakespeare's comedy into ballet. I only have the headline, so I can't describe the choreography or the music. But I know you love dance and Shakespeare, so I wanted to flag it, and it does raise an interesting teaching question. Midsummer Night's Dream isn't on your programme, but the idea of a story told without words is a fine way to get students thinking about what language adds. If a ballet can carry confusion, desire and transformation through movement alone, what does Shakespeare's verse do that dancers cannot? You could pair that with a moment of Twelfth Night, where the language is doing a great deal of the work, and ask students to imagine how they would show it without speech.

So, to gather the week together: a Butler excerpt for ecocriticism, an Atwood staging for retold myth, an Austen adaptation interview for questions of fidelity, and a lot of Hamlet, from a Gothic-minded interview to a trailer you may wish to preview. And that's your BFI corner for today, Yamuna; I hope something in it makes its way into a lesson, or at least into a quiet cup of tea.

Good morning, Yamuna. This morning's good news has a lot of roots in it, in trees, orchards and neighbourhoods, with a little music and bronze along the way.

Let me begin with the forests, where the news is quite encouraging. Positive News has a profile of Susana Afrifa Ankrah, a cocoa farmer in Ghana, who shows how protecting trees can support a farmer's livelihood and help a community adapt to a changing climate. It is told in her own words, and it is a grounded, human piece, the sort you might read aloud to a class to show how a strong first-person voice can carry an argument without any fuss.

Further east, Good News Network reports that Indonesia has paused, and perhaps ended, what was described as the world's largest deforestation project. The country reached rice self-sufficiency about three years earlier than planned, and so around four million acres of rainforest, swamps and peatlands may now be spared. I should say that their future is still unclear, so this is a reprieve rather than a guarantee, but it is a real one.

And from the South Pacific comes a very concrete result. One year after invasive rats and pigs were removed from Nu'utele Island in Samoa, the forests, wildlife and food sources are already recovering strongly. It is a Key Biodiversity Area, and the report speaks of an explosion of native wildlife. Positive News, in its weekly roundup of what went right, adds another note of hope, saying that rewilding is offering a future to low-lying islands. The same roundup mentions a basic income trial showing promise, and a Bangladeshi factory winning an award, though each is only touched on briefly.

Now to the land closer to the table, and a few stories that I think you would enjoy as someone who loves a producers' market. In Kansas City, the Giving Grove has built a network of free community orchards that has become a national model. At Kansas City Academy, students pick jujubes straight from the trees during their lunch break. I like that picture very much: food, learning and neighbourhood life all happening in the same place, with no one having to be persuaded.

On a similar theme, Good News Network says that Europe's Spar supermarket group is beginning wide-scale commercial tests of heritage and alpine apple varieties, many with unusual names that reflect their histories. It is still only a test, so we will have to wait and see whether those apples reach the shelves, but it is a pleasing nod to old orchards and to biodiversity. It made me think of the names alone as small pieces of poetry.

Also from Good News Network, a study from the University of Bari in Italy found that grapevines grown beneath solar panels produced bigger, healthier grapes, while the panels generated clean energy at the same time. The technique is called agrivoltaics, and it suggests that farmland can do two jobs at once. For a European wine-growing landscape, it is a practical and well-evidenced idea.

Let me turn now to art and culture, where there are some interesting threads. The Guardian reviews Ibrahim Mahama's exhibition at the Fondation Cartier in Paris. In it, a crumbling bottle plant has been rebuilt, and Asante stools sit alongside it, to explore Ghana after colonialism. The reviewer asks whether the future might be Ghana-shaped, and finds a sense of hope in the show. It is a good example of art and history speaking to one another, and it might be worth a visit if you are next in Paris. It also connects, quite by chance, to Susana Afrifa Ankrah's story, as Ghana appears twice in this briefing.

Also in Paris, Reasons to be Cheerful writes about what it calls artivism. Around two hundred musicians and volunteers, mostly young, gathered in front of the Hôtel de Ville for a performance led by a figure in a Darth Vader costume. I only have an excerpt that cuts off early, so I cannot tell you what the cause or the wider aims are, but the image of an orchestra and a Sith lord outside a town hall is hard to forget.

Closer to home, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that the Bedouin association C'est Normal is introducing its Savoyard neighbours to dance. I only have the headline, so I cannot give you details, but it sounds like a warm story of cultural exchange in our own corner of the Alps, and perhaps something to look out for locally.

And in Atlanta, a twenty-nine-foot bronze statue of Cyrus the Great was installed this week. He was the Persian king who ruled about two thousand five hundred years ago, and he is often linked to an early charter of tolerance. Good News Network says the story of the people who brought the statue there gives it a nice human angle alongside the historical one.

Finally, a story of kindness that I rather like, and which would make a good opening for a short story. In Mineral Wells, Texas, Dale, who is eighty-six, has been welding a sixty-two-foot steel boat in his front yard since nineteen eighty-seven. Strangers are now stepping in to help him move closer to his long-held dream. There is something Melvillean, or perhaps Steinbeckian, about a man and his boat, and it is good to know that this time a community has turned up to help him finish it.

That is the news for today, Yamuna, and I hope it leaves you with something to savour alongside your morning coffee.
good.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. This morning's good news has a lot of green in it, from forests and orchards to a few warm stories about people, and some of it comes from very close to home.

Let me begin with trees, and with a voice I think you'll enjoy. Positive News has a profile of Susana Afrifa Ankrah, a cocoa farmer in Ghana. She shows how protecting forests and supporting farmers' livelihoods can go hand in hand, and how that helps whole communities adapt to a changing climate. What I like about the piece is that it lets her speak for herself. It's a grounded, human story, told by someone who works the land, rather than a lecture about it. If you ever want a short, real narrator for a class on voice and perspective, it might be worth a look. Her argument is simple and quietly persuasive: the trees are not in the way of the farm, they are part of the future of the farm.

That thought carries neatly to Indonesia. Good News Network reports that what was described as the world's largest deforestation project has been paused, and perhaps ended altogether. The reason is that the country reached rice self-sufficiency about three years earlier than planned. So the land that was meant to help feed the nation was no longer needed for that purpose. That may spare around four million acres of rainforest, swamps and peatlands. I should be honest that their future is still unclear, and a pause is not the same as a promise. But four million acres is an enormous area, and it's rare to hear of a vast project stopping because it has already achieved its goal.

From there, a smaller place with a very concrete result. Also from Good News Network: on Nu'utele Island in Samoa, invasive rats and pigs were removed, and one year on, the forests, the wildlife and the food sources are already showing strong recovery. The island sits within a Key Biodiversity Area, which is a designation for places of particular importance to wildlife. The report describes an explosion of native life, and I find that phrase rather lovely, because it suggests how quickly nature can answer when the pressure is lifted. It's a reminder that conservation is not always about heroic, slow struggle. Sometimes it's a decision, a careful operation, and then a year of watching something return.

Positive News also has its weekly roundup, called What went right this week, and one item fits this theme well: rewilding is offering hope to low-lying islands. The piece is brisk, so I can't tell you more than that, but it pairs naturally with the Samoan story. Two island stories in one morning, both pointing the same way.

Now to the fields and orchards, where the news is a little more practical, and in places very local in flavour.

Good News Network reports on a study from the University of Bari, in southern Italy. Researchers found that grapevines grown under solar panels, an approach called agrivoltaics, produced bigger and healthier grapes, while the same land also generated clean energy. I think this is a clever idea, because it avoids the old question of whether a field should grow food or make power. Here the panels and the vines share the space, and the vines seem to benefit. For anyone who looks out over a valley of vineyards and orchards, as you do from the Grésivaudan, it is easy to picture how this might one day matter close to home, though of course I would not claim that it's coming to Belledonne tomorrow.

Staying with orchards, Good News Network also tells us that Spar, the European supermarket group, is beginning wide-scale commercial tests of heritage and alpine apple varieties. These are apples with unusual names, names that reflect their histories, and I do love the idea of a supermarket shelf carrying apples that sound as though they belong in a novel. It's still a test, so we don't yet know whether these varieties will stay on the shelves. But for biodiversity, it matters that old varieties are being given a chance to be tasted and bought, rather than being kept alive only in a few gardens and old orchards. If you spot any of them at a producers' market this autumn, they may well be the same kind of fruit, in spirit at least.

And a third orchard story, this one from the United States. The Optimist Daily writes about The Giving Grove in Kansas City, a network of free community orchards that has become a national model. One image from it has stayed with me: at Kansas City Academy, students pick jujubes from trees during their lunch break. Imagine a school lunch hour in which you can simply walk out and pick fruit from a tree. It's a lovely example of food, education and neighbourhood life working together, and it shows how a few trees can change the feel of a place. As a teacher, you might smile at the thought of pupils learning in the shade of something that actually bears fruit.

Let me move now to art and culture, where there are a few items with real depth.

The Guardian's art and design section reviews Ibrahim Mahama's exhibition at the Fondation Cartier in Paris, under a title that asks why a crumbling bottle plant has been rebuilt there. The show features a rebuilt factory and Asante stools, and it explores Ghana after colonialism. The reviewer suggests the future may be Ghana-shaped, and finds a real sense of hope in the work. What interests me is the way the exhibition connects art to history, using objects and a building to carry a story that a textbook might struggle to hold. I think it's the sort of thing you often enjoy, where a physical space becomes a kind of narrative, and you walk into it as you would walk into a novel. I also notice a quiet echo with this morning's other Ghanaian story. Different worlds, a farmer and an artist, but both imagining a future that grows out of Ghana's own soil and history.

On the subject of history made visible, Good News Network reports that a twenty-nine-foot bronze statue of Cyrus the Great was installed in Atlanta this week. Cyrus was a Persian king, often linked to an early charter of tolerance, from about two and a half thousand years ago. The story behind the statue is also about the people who brought it there, and that gives it a human angle as well as a historical one. I don't have more detail than that, but there is something striking about a figure from the ancient world arriving, in bronze, in a modern American city, carrying an idea about tolerance with him.

Back in Paris, Reasons to be Cheerful has a piece on what it calls artivism, art as activism. The scene it opens with is quite something: around two hundred mostly young musicians and volunteers gathered in front of the Hôtel de Ville for a performance led by a figure in a Darth Vader costume. I have to be frank, the excerpt cuts off, so I can't tell you what the cause is or what wider aims the group has. But the picture itself is vivid, young people, instruments, and a solemn black helmet in front of one of the grandest buildings in Paris. If you're curious, it may be worth reading the full piece to see where it goes.

Closer to home, and in a warmer key, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that the Bedouin association C'est Normal is introducing its Savoyard neighbours to dance. I only have the headline, so I can't describe the sessions or say where exactly they take place. Still, even the headline tells a nice story: an association bringing its own culture to the people next door, and the neighbours stepping into it through movement. Given your love of dance, I thought it worth flagging, and it may be worth a look in the regional pages if you'd like to know more.

Finally, two stories of simple human kindness.

Good News Network tells of Dale, who is eighty-six and lives in Mineral Wells, Texas. Since nineteen eighty-seven he has been welding a sixty-two-foot steel boat in his front yard. That is nearly forty years of patient work, in a yard, a long way from the sea. Strangers are now helping him move towards his long-held dream. I find it a charming story, with a character any novelist would be glad to invent: stubborn, hopeful, a little eccentric, and then rewarded by the unexpected generosity of people who never knew him. It's the sort of tale that makes you think about the quiet projects people carry for decades, and how a community can notice them at last.

And to close the circle on Positive News, the same weekly roundup contains two more brief items. A basic income trial is showing promise, and a factory in Bangladesh has won an award. The report is short, so I can't give you the detail behind either, but they sit well alongside the rewilding item I mentioned earlier, a small cluster of good news from different corners of the world.

So that's the morning: farmers and forests in Ghana and Indonesia, an island recovering in Samoa, vines drinking in the shade of solar panels, old apples heading for the shelves, a rebuilt factory in Paris, a bronze king in Atlanta, and an eighty-six-year-old with a boat. I hope something in there keeps you company today, perhaps with an apple in your hand.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Friday the twenty-third of October, and here is a gentle round-up of France over the last couple of days, with a stormy start and a good deal of culture to follow.

Let's begin with the weather, since it's the most practical news. The Local France reports that Storm Austen has swept across western France, leaving hundreds of thousands of households without electricity and seriously disrupting transport this Friday morning. Nothing in the report points to Grenoble specifically, but if you or anyone you know is travelling towards the west today, it's worth checking before setting off.

French health authorities announced on Thursday that the Shamonda virus, which usually affects livestock, has been found in a human for the first time in France. The Local says the case was a severely immunocompromised patient, who died earlier this month. It is a first and therefore notable, but the details we have are limited to that single case.

One person involved says the pupils "tell us about their lives in great detail", and the report looks at how those contributions are actually read and handled. He wrote Coin Locker Babies, and franceinfo describes his work as an unsparing view of Japanese society. It's a dark, vivid and uncompromising kind of fiction, and the news may be a good prompt to pick up that novel, or to return to it if you already know it.

There's a striking story in The Guardian about music under pressure. The conductor Étienne Jarrier and his New World Orchestra were playing in Place de la République in Paris last week, and the musicians kept playing until teargas was fired at them. Jarrier's reported reaction gives the piece its headline: an orchestra being gassed, he says, should be an alarm signal. The wider backdrop is protest and policing, but at its heart is a picture that stays in the mind: a group of musicians continuing to play as the gas arrives.

On a lighter and more graceful note, there's dance. Today in Angers, the Olympic ice dance champions Laurence Fournier Beaudry and Guillaume Cizeron return to competition at the Grand Prix de France. In an interview with franceinfo, they say they want to explore new ways of moving and to put the artistic side at the heart of their new season, pushing their sport towards greater artistic modernity. Given your love of dance documentaries, that might be worth following, as a performance as much as a sporting event.

I'll leave the story to the article rather than guess at it.

Finally, La Mire's daily video, the edition of the twenty-second of October. It's a round-up of French television, and today's is firmly current affairs. Do expect a sober, news-heavy watch rather than a light one. The bakery testimony is probably the most human part, if you only have time for a little of it.

So, to sum up the shape of the day: a stormy morning in the west, a first-of-its-kind health report, a thoughtful look at how lycéens are being heard, and a rich helping of music, dance, fiction and language. I hope your Friday is gentler than the weather in Brittany and beyond.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Friday the twenty-third of October, and here is a gentle round-up of France from the last two days, with weather and travel first, then schools, then a good deal of music, dance and words.

Let's start with the weather, since it's the most practical news. The Local France reports that Storm Austen has hit western France, leaving hundreds of thousands of households without electricity and seriously disrupting transport this Friday morning. This is the west, a long way from Belledonne and the Grésivaudan, so it shouldn't touch your own day. But if you have friends or family out that way, or a journey planned that crosses the country, it's worth checking before anyone sets off. Storms like this tend to leave knock-on delays for a while, so patience is the sensible approach.

A more sombre piece of news comes from the health authorities. On Thursday they announced that the Shamonda virus, which usually affects livestock, has been found in a human for the first time in France. The Local France says the case was a severely immunocompromised patient, who died earlier this month. That is the extent of what I have, so I'll leave it there rather than guess at more. It is a first, which is why it made the news, but the details so far are few.

Now to schools, which will be close to your own working life. franceinfo has been behind the scenes of a national consultation platform where lycéens describe the problems they see in their schools and suggest solutions. One of the people quoted says the pupils tell them about their daily lives in great detail, and the report asks how those contributions are actually handled once they're submitted. It's a practical question, and an interesting one: what happens to a teenager's account of their own school once it enters a large system? You'll know better than most how articulate and observant a seconde or première class can be when somebody actually asks them what they think. It would be worth listening to your pupils' view of this, if the subject comes up in the classroom or the corridor.

From there, to the arts, and I'll begin with a story that is both moving and a little troubling. The Guardian reports on the conductor Étienne Jarrier and the New World Orchestra. Last week, the musicians were playing in the Place de la République in Paris, and they kept playing until teargas was fired at them. The conductor's own words, which give the piece its title, are that an orchestra being gassed should be an alarm signal. The backdrop is protest and policing in the capital, which I'll mention only because it's the setting, not because I want to draw you into the politics. What stays with me is the image: a group of people with instruments, in one of Paris's best-known squares, continuing to play as the air turns hostile. Music has so often been the thing people turn to when words feel inadequate, and the Guardian treats the musicians as activists in their own right. If you like documentaries about classical music, this has something of that spirit, the idea of an orchestra as more than a concert-hall institution.

On a lighter, more graceful note, there is dance on ice. Today, Friday the twenty-third of October, in Angers, Laurence Fournier Beaudry and Guillaume Cizeron return to competition at the Grand Prix de France. They are the Olympic ice dance champions, and franceinfo has been talking to them about their new season. Their stated aim is to explore new ways of moving, and to place the artistic side at the heart of what they do, pushing their sport towards greater artistic modernity. Since you enjoy dance, this one may be worth watching for its own sake. Ice dance is a curious form: it sits between sport and choreography, and a pair who talk openly about wanting to widen the vocabulary of movement is a pair worth watching. Whether they succeed is something we'll learn as the season goes on, but it's good to hear athletes speak about their work in terms of art.

Staying with dance, The Local's weekly La Belle Vie column looks at French Halloween, at autumn exhibitions, and at the idea of getting back into dancing as an adult. It also makes a case for small pleasures after a hard week. The text is brief, but the themes suit you well: the exhibitions are a reminder that autumn is the season when galleries and museums put their best programmes forward, and the dancing theme is a charming counterpart to the ice dancers. Taking up dance again as an adult is something many people dream of and few attempt, so it's nice to see it treated as a reasonable thing to do. As for Halloween, it's coming up next weekend, and the column explores how the French have taken it on in their own way. If you fancy a trip to a local exhibition over the half-term period, it may be a nudge in the right direction.

Now a sad note from the world of books. franceinfo reports that the Japanese novelist and filmmaker Ryu Murakami has died at the age of seventy-four. He is best known as the author of Coin Locker Babies, which in French is Les Bébés de la consigne automatique. franceinfo describes his work as offering an unsparing view of Japanese society. That phrase tells you something about the kind of writer he was: someone who looked directly at what others preferred to overlook. I should say, too, that he is not the Murakami most readers think of first, so if a pupil mentions Murakami, it's worth checking which one. His death feels like a fitting moment to revisit his fiction, particularly if you like novels where the strength of a voice carries you into a world you don't know. It might also be interesting for an older class as a contrast with more familiar narrators.

And finally, two small pleasures for a teacher of language. The Local France has its French Expression of the Day, and this time there are two. The first is a phrase that sounds like nonsense and, as the piece cheerfully admits, is nonsense: Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres. It nonetheless has a particular backstory, and that's what makes it worth a look. It's the sort of thing that fascinates anyone who enjoys how language travels, and how a phrase can acquire a life of its own regardless of its sense. The second is bouc émissaire. This is the French for scapegoat, and the Local explains that it shares its biblical origins with the English equivalent. The word bouc simply means a billy goat, so the image is the same on both sides of the Channel: the animal that carried the community's sins into the wilderness. For a literature teacher, this is a lovely example of how a story from an ancient text lives on inside everyday speech, and how often we use a phrase without remembering that it began as a ritual. It would make a neat little starter for a lesson on idiom, or on the Bible's influence on English and French alike.

Lastly, the daily video from La Mire, the round-up of French television for the twenty-second of October. This one is a news-heavy watch. It covers the clean-up in Paris after the violence of the seventeenth of October, a shop-owner's account of a ransacked bakery, and the responses from the police and the government. I'd treat it as sober viewing, rather than a relaxing one. The bakery owner's testimony is probably the part that will stay with you, because it puts a human face on events that are otherwise discussed in large and abstract terms. If you'd rather keep your morning light, it will keep until later.

So that's France for today: a storm in the west, a first for a virus, teenagers being heard, an orchestra that wouldn't stop playing, and a good many words to enjoy. I hope your Friday leaves room for one small pleasure of your own.
