Good morning, Yamuna. It is a quieter two days for streaming than for the stage, so I'll start with the thrillers, then turn to the dance and music reviews that caught my eye.

Netflix first, because three of the stories are about thrillers on your platform. The bad news is that the reports are short on detail, and none of them gives me a title, so please take them as pointers and not recommendations.

Comic Book Resources reports that a new six-part Netflix thriller has become the number one show in the world, with one hundred and fifty-six million hours viewed. That is a very large number, and six episodes is a manageable commitment. But the text names no title and describes no plot, so I can't tell you whether it is a slow-burning mystery or something louder. It is worth keeping an eye on Netflix's top ten to see what is sitting at the summit.

MovieWeb has two further stories. One is about a new twenty-episode sci-fi action thriller, which reportedly climbed to the top of the streaming charts within a single day of release. Twenty episodes is a long haul, and the report offers little beyond the ranking, so I would treat it as one for a rainy weekend, if at all. The other concerns a four-part sci-fi thriller on Netflix, which MovieWeb says is drawing big audiences, and the headline links it to a rival streamer's most-watched show. Again, the detail is thin. If you want something short, a four-part series is the neatest of the three.

If you would rather plan than chase the charts, TVGuide.com has put together a complete guide to the autumn 2026 television season. The text I have is sparse, so I can't pick out particular titles for you, but it may be a useful place to look for new thrillers and dramas, and to check which platform each one lands on.

One more thriller note, with a caveat. Men's Journal has a roundup of what is known about season seven of Slow Horses, the spy thriller on Apple TV. Apple TV isn't among your platforms, and the piece gives no detail beyond the headline, so I mention it only because you enjoy the genre. If it ever turns up somewhere you can watch it, it is one to remember.

Now to dance, where The Guardian has two pieces. Neither is a broadcast, as far as the text says. They are reviews of live productions in London, so think of them as a window onto what is happening on stage.

At Sadler's Wells East, the Guardian critic writes about Tellus, a new work by Dickson Mbi. It draws on his Cameroonian heritage, and the score he composed himself is central to the piece. The headline calls it a mighty cry for a goddess to help the Earth, and the review describes a confident, expressive work that shows Mbi as a bold force in dance. For someone who loves the way a story can travel between cultures, and how music and movement carry meaning, it sounds like a fascinating piece.

The Guardian also reports on a new staging of The Snowman, which began with Raymond Briggs's picture book and Howard Blake's score. This version is directed by Will Tuckett, with a hi-tech refresh and a new Saint Nick. The headline mentions a Hot Santa, a touch of Raging Bull, and a Toy Story vibe, which gives you a sense of how playfully it has been reimagined for a new generation. As someone who likes to see a story move from page to music to stage, you may enjoy the thought of this one, even from a distance.

Finally, two classical music reviews, again from The Guardian. The first covers the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra at the Lighthouse in Poole, conducted by Mark Wigglesworth. The programme pairs Tippett, Vaughan Williams, Adès and Sibelius, and the Tippett is singled out as the highlight. The reviewer's headline describes the phrasing as having hospital corners, which suggests playing that is precise and very neatly turned, though the review also leaves you in no doubt about where the real excitement lay.

The second is an album review. Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic have recorded Bartók's The Miraculous Mandarin suite alongside The Wooden Prince, the earlier ballet, which is rooted in Hungarian folk music. The reviewer praises the vivid colours and astute pacing, and calls the performances taut and dramatically alert. Both works began life as stage pieces, so it is a nice reminder that a great deal of Bartók is storytelling in sound. If you are looking for something to listen to on a grey evening in Les Adrets, this sounds like a rewarding choice.

So, to sum up. The streaming news is mostly about charts and not much about content, so I'd wait for firmer details before committing to any of the Netflix thrillers. The stage and concert reviews are richer, and they might help you decide what to listen to or look out for.

Enjoy the weekend, Yamuna, and may your evening viewing have a good plot.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter couple of days for the screen than for the stage, so today's briefing leans on a few thrillers climbing the Netflix charts, then turns to dance and music that you may want to keep an eye out for.

Let me start with the thrillers, since that is where your platforms are busiest. Netflix is having a run of them, though I should be honest at the outset that the reports are thin. Most are chart stories rather than reviews, so what I can offer is a set of pointers, not recommendations I can vouch for.

The biggest number first. Comic Book Resources reports that a new six-part Netflix thriller is now the number one show in the world, with one hundred and fifty-six million hours viewed. That is a very large audience for a series of only six episodes. The piece, as it reached me, gives no title and no plot, so I can't tell you what it is about, who is in it, or whether it is any good. What I can say is that six episodes is a manageable shape. If you like a thriller you can finish over a long weekend, it's worth looking at the Netflix top ten this morning and seeing which six-part series sits at the head of it. A show that has gathered that much attention that quickly may also be one your older pupils are already talking about.

The second is a different kind of animal. MovieWeb reports that a new Netflix science-fiction action thriller, running to twenty episodes, has risen to the top of the streaming charts within a day of release. Twenty episodes is a long commitment, and the report offers little beyond the ranking, so I don't know the setting, the characters or the tone. Science fiction and action are not always where your taste lies, since you tend to prefer strong characters and narrators, and a story you can step into without any preparation. A series of that length does at least have room to build people rather than just plot, but that is a hope, not something the report tells us. I would treat this one as a maybe, and wait for a few proper reviews before giving it your evenings.

The third is also from MovieWeb, and it is shorter again. Netflix has a four-part science-fiction thriller that is reportedly drawing big audiences, and the headline says it has found a hit alongside a rival streamer's most-watched show. The text I have is only the headline, so there is very little detail to pass on. But four episodes is the most compact of the three. If you are in the mood for something that will not swallow your week, it may be the easiest to try. Again, I can't say whether it is thoughtful or merely fast, so it is a name to look up, not a promise.

So the honest summary of the Netflix news is this. There are three thrillers, of six, twenty and four episodes, all doing well in the charts, and none that I can describe to you in any real detail. If one of them turns out to have a memorable central character or a voice worth following, I will happily tell you more when the reviews arrive.

There is also a broader resource, which is TVGuide dot com's complete guide to the autumn 2026 television season. It sets out to cover everything worth knowing about what to watch this season. The text I have is thin and most of the titles are unknown to me, so I can't pick out highlights. But if you like to plan your viewing for the darker months, and you do seem to like having a few things lined up for the evenings when the light goes early above the Grésivaudan, it may be a useful place to browse for new thrillers and dramas, and to see what is arriving on your platforms.

One more thriller worth a mention, though not on your platforms. Men's Journal has a roundup of what is known about season seven of Slow Horses, the spy thriller on Apple TV. Apple TV is not among the services you use, and the piece as I have it gives nothing beyond the headline. So I mention it only so that the name is not a surprise if someone brings it up. There is no action for you to take.

Now to dance and the stage. Nothing in these reports says that either production is being filmed or streamed, so think of them as things to follow, perhaps in case they travel or are recorded later, and as good reading in themselves.

The Guardian has a review of Tellus, the new work by Dickson Mbi, at Sadler's Wells East in London. The headline calls it a mighty cry for a goddess to help Earth, and says it proves Mbi is a bold force in dance. The critic says the piece draws on his Cameroonian heritage, and that the score, which he composed himself, is central to a confident and expressive evening. I like the idea that the same person has shaped both the movement and the music, because it suggests a piece where the two are not simply laid on top of each other. For someone who enjoys dance documentaries, and who likes work you can enter without needing to know the culture first, the review is a good account of a choreographer speaking from a specific heritage in a way the critic found direct and strong. It is worth reading for the language alone, and worth remembering as a name.

The second dance story has a very different mood, and you may enjoy it in a gentler way. The Guardian reports on a new staging of Raymond Briggs's The Snowman, directed by Will Tuckett. The headline promises a Hot Santa, a touch of Raging Bull and a Toy Story vibe, which tells you the production has a sense of humour about itself. The report says the staging has had a hi-tech refresh and brings in a new Saint Nick, all aimed at a new generation. What appeals to me about it, for you, is the lineage. It begins with Briggs's picture book, where the story is told in pictures, and it carries Howard Blake's score, so it is a tale that has already moved across several forms and is now moving again. You often draw on those links between images and words and music, so it may be a charming thing to mention to a class, particularly with the season coming. I would not call it an urgent watch, since I have no word on whether it will be filmed, but as a story that keeps being retold in new media it is a pleasing one.

Finally, two pieces of classical music, one a concert and one a recording.

The Guardian reviews a Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra concert at the Lighthouse in Poole, conducted by Mark Wigglesworth. The programme pairs Tippett, Vaughan Williams, Adès and Sibelius, which is a handsome mix of British voices with a Finnish master. The Tippett is singled out as the highlight. The headline describes the phrasing as having hospital corners, which is a lovely and slightly teasing image of playing that is very neat and precisely made. I can't tell you from the review alone how warm or how daring the evening was, but the critic clearly admired the Tippett, and the programme is an interesting one for anyone who likes to hear how British music of different generations sits together alongside something from further north. If any of it is broadcast, I will let you know.

The second is a recording. The Guardian reviews an album of Bartók from Edward Gardner and the London Philharmonic, containing the Miraculous Mandarin Suite and The Wooden Prince. The Wooden Prince is the earlier ballet, and the review notes that it is rooted in Hungarian folk music. The reviewer praises the performances as taut and dramatically alert, with vivid colours and astute pacing, and I like that last phrase in particular, because pacing is just what makes a ballet score feel like a story and not just a sequence of pieces. Both works were written for the stage, so listening to them is a way of hearing dance without seeing it. If you enjoy documentaries about dance and classical music, this album is a lovely companion to them, and it might be pleasant to put on while you are marking or cooking, with the ear following the narrative while the eye does something else.

So, to gather it up. For something to watch tonight, the safest advice is to look at the Netflix charts for those three thrillers, and perhaps start with the shortest, while holding off on the long science-fiction one until there is more to go on. For browsing, the autumn television guide may help you plan. For reading and keeping in mind, there are Dickson Mbi's Tellus and the new Snowman. And for listening, the Bournemouth concert and the Bartók album are both well reviewed and rich in story.

That is all for this morning, and I hope you find something lovely to settle down with when the evening comes.
